💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.
  • Pollo AI⁠(opens in a new window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise.
  • “We want to do for video what Canva did for design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.

Pollo AI⁠(opens in a new window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise. Even with generative AI, creators and marketers can struggle to navigate different tools and choose between models to get the result they want. Some may even abandon their projects in frustration.

“We want to do for video what Canva did for design. We want to make it easy enough that more people can actually use it, not just the ones who already know how,” explains Bill Zhu, the founder and CEO of Pollo AI. Today, Pollo AI serves more than 26 million users who use the platform to create videos, ads, and visual content.

The team’s first breakthrough was video templates. Now, 30% of creator sessions start from these templates or trending-format workflows. Building on this success, the tech giant’s latest offering is Pollo Agent. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user.

Industry observers note that pollo Agent interprets the user’s rough ideas and visual references, and then develops storylines, scene flows, and scripts. CTO Peter Zhou claims OpenAI models stood out for their ability to understand ambiguous creative inputs and their multimodal capability, sharing: “GPT‑5.6 performed especially well there.” The team also remarked they value the OpenAI API’s stability and release cadence.

To balance reasoning depth, speed, and cost, Pollo AI uses GPT‑5.6 for routing and GPT‑6 Astra for more challenging work, such as developing a narrative or planning scene revisions. This model mix lets the system match the level of reasoning to the task based on the user’s prompt. Pollo AI reports that people spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity.

According to recent reports, pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals.

Pollo AI’s primary owners are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content rapidly and easily too.

Pollo’s Photo to Video Ads tool in its Marketing Studio suite uses OpenAI models to turn a still image and prompt into a short video. It’s designed to help small businesses and DTC brands generate product ads for social media in minutes rather than days.

One Pollo AI user wanted to use a product photo to make a fragrance ad that felt luxurious. The static photo alone could not convey that mood, and a professional video shoot was beyond their budget.

In a recent development, using Photo to Video Ad, the user turned their starting image into a roughly 15-second video ad. The tool generated velvet textures, warm spotlights, and close-ups of the bottle to establish the mood across the sequence and ended it with the fragrance framed against deep red fabric.

Another customer, a jewelry brand, wanted a bold editorial campaign image, but its budget could not stretch to a high-concept studio shoot.

According to recent reports, using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, the brand was able to turn its creative vision of its statement jewelry on a model seated beside a cheetah into reality. The tool framed the scene with dark drapery and warm lighting and ensured that the brand’s jewelry products were highly visible.

The customer got a finished luxury campaign visual with lower production effort, time, and cost compared to live shoot.

Sources indicate that pollo AI also makes it easy for customers to start with a product photo and leverage OpenAI models to turn it into an image that’s far more creative. For example, a beverage brand wanted its peach soda to feel playful and imaginative in an advertising campaign, but a standard studio product shot could not capture what the team had in mind.

Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, which brings sharper details and faster generation to creative workflows, the team transformed a simple bottle image into a snowy miniature landscape, complete with a train, lizards, and sparkling droplets. The finished image created a playful scene the brand could use in its campaign.

Pollo wants AI video to become part of everyday content creation over the next 12 months. For Zhu, that depends on making it even easier to turn an idea into an asset ready to post, test, or use in a campaign, something Pollo AI is enabled to deliver with the continued improvement of OpenAI models and image generation.

“We think the AI shift in content creation will favor products that make creation more repeatable from the start, with stronger formats, less trial and error, and a simpler workflow around the models themselves,” he says.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.
  • Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.
  • Over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.

Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.

Over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization. In each case, work that used to rely on specialists and take days can now be done by anyone and is complete in minutes. Recruiters skip days of market research, business people describe an outcome instead of hunting for a report, and technical leads build tools that used to take a full team months.

Sources indicate that the talent acquisition team used ChatGPT Work to build a talent market intelligence tool that takes a job description, researches comparable roles, benchmarks compensation, and assesses the talent pool across relevant locations. The tool arms the recruiter with valuable information that they need going into a conversation with the hiring manager, information that previously took 2–4 days to compile.

“We’ve gone from zero to a hundred,” indicates Jan Ackerman, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Talent Acquisition at Oracle. “Now we’re able to sit down and prep for about 15 to 20 minutes using the tool that we’ve built using [ChatGPT] Work.”.

Not only is the process faster, but it’s also more consistent. Recruiters used to run the intake process differently from one search to the next, but with the talent market intelligence tool, the process is consistent, so every hiring manager has the same quality of data and insights, no matter which recruiter they worked with.

According to recent reports, the Oracle Applications Lab team, which helps run many of Oracle’s core business processes, built an ontology of the firm’s objects, relationships, and rules, so a plain-language business question can be turned into a reliable SQL query with Codex. A business user describes the outcome they want, and Codex decides which internal systems to call, gathers the information, and returns an analysis, a report, or an application.

Industry observers note that that’s a change from how work used to get done. Lam said one user came to him after asking a question that would normally have taken her a couple of hours to answer. She told Lam, “With the upcoming tool, I put in the request and got a response almost immediately.” When she checked the result against the old manual process, the numbers matched exactly.

According to recent reports, in production engineering, site reliability engineers use Codex to gather relevant context about an incident and automatically pull up the right playbook. SREs spend more time guiding decisions and less time hunting for information. “A typical simple incident that used to take an hour to resolve can now be handled in minutes,” notes Lam.

Even as Codex takes on more of the work, Lam is careful to note that none of this runs on autopilot. Someone still has to make sure the underlying system is built right.

While AI builds the tools, the people are still responsible for the output. A few lessons stand out:.

Give the correct guardrails. “You have to still be very responsible about your system design, your architecture, your security, and how you would like Codex to structure the code for you,” says Lam.

In a recent development, provide prototypes instead of specs. “Normally, I put [my idea] down on paper, but now I put it down in a prototype,” says Barry Shilmover, Vice President and Technical Advisor to the CIO.

Industry observers note that own the code. “If you don’t work alongside Codex, you’re going to get into a situation of having lots of code that is not going to be maintainable,” notes Lam.

The Oracle team is completely shifting how the company operates with AI. Across recruiting, analytics, and engineering, each line of business described an outcome and let Codex and ChatGPT handle how the work gets done. With thousands of ChatGPT and Codex consumers already, Oracle employees use AI across countless work tasks. As Shilmover puts it, “I don’t know what the answer is because I don’t know what my next problem to solve will be. I just know that one of the first things I’ll do is I’ll leverage Codex to do that.”.

📅 09 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1132 w)

Asana cuts model costs 76x in browser tests with GPT-6.1 Sol

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1132 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.
  • Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
  • Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.

Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Average estimated model cost with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

With GPT‑6 Astra in Codex running experiments, Asana optimized its browser agent’s workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol to run 76x cheaper and 5x faster.

Asana helps customers automate work across business applications through StackAI⁠(opens in a new window), a platform it acquired⁠(opens in a new window). Using StackAI, customers can build workflows that navigate websites, fill out forms, and gather information without writing code. At Asana’s scale, small inefficiencies in these workflows add up.

Sources indicate that asana’s StackAI CTO, Frank Hidalgo, PhD, set out to make the browser agent faster and cheaper to run. He directed GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to investigate the agent, test improvements, and compare the results. Work he estimates would have taken one to two months by hand took about a week.

Sources indicate that asana’s 144-run study⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) tested GPT‑6.1 Sol and three other frontier models, called here Models A, B and C. The optimized workflow that emerged on GPT‑6.1 Sol averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, 76x cheaper and 5x faster than the original production setup on Model B.

According to recent reports, to move quickly, Hidalgo started by using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to map the codebase and explain how the agent built each model request. GPT‑6 Astra discovered that the agent cached its fixed instructions and tool definitions, but not the growing history of page text and screenshots it gathered, so every request resent that history at full price.

According to recent reports, the agent also dropped older screenshots and trimmed text at nearly every step. Each edit altered the history, so caching the history alone would not have helped, and losing those facts could require the agent to revisit pages it had already read.

Hidalgo reviewed GPT‑6 Astra’s proposed fixes and selected three to test:.

Extending caching to the agent’s browsing history.

Increasing the amount of text it could retain.

Removing screenshots in batches rather than at every step.

GPT‑6 Astra began with quick tests to establish which variables mattered. Because the code was not designed for controlled experiments, it then refactored the code so one frontend and backend could support many workflows in parallel, each with its own settings.

In a recent development, astra conducted the full study: history budgets of 120,000 and 480,000 characters and six caching and screenshot policies, each tested three times on each of the four models (see the table below). The best-performing policy allowed screenshots to accumulate to 20 before cutting back to the most recent one. This kept earlier history unchanged for longer stretches between removals. Combined with the larger history budget, it became the optimized workflow. Each configuration performed the same task: collecting six fields for each of 32 books from a public demo catalog, representative of what some Asana customers run in StackAI.

A smaller, less expensive model from another frontier lab, released Fall 2025.

The model originally used in production, from the same lab as Model A, released Summer 2026.

An updated version of Model B, released Fall 2026.

Sources indicate that GPT‑6 Astra ran the workflows and examined the requests, usage records and outputs, and separate model sessions reviewed the work. Every session’s requests, data traces and results were recorded in Command⁠(opens in a newly introduced window), Asana’s software delivery platform, so the team could review the complete study afterward. From Command, the findings were turned into tickets, then pull requests, and the changes went to production.

It has been revealed that for Model B, the optimization reduced estimated model cost from at least $36.21 (some original runs reached the step limit before they finished) to $1.24 per run, a reduction of 29x. The optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol was 2.6x cheaper still, at $0.47. Every run in the optimized workflow completed the task and returned the correct answer.

Means of 3 runs. ≥: the baseline includes capped runs, so its mean is a lower bound.

Sources indicate that the two right folds compare against Model B optimized. Model B ran in phase 1, Model C and Sol 6.1 in phase 2 of the same study (dotted line).

On GPT‑6.1 Sol alone, with the larger history budget, the new caching and screenshot policy reduced cost 4x, from $1.97 to $0.47 per run. Each call was about 3x cheaper, because 89% of the input came from cache at 5% of the uncached price. Runs also became faster: at least 22.5 minutes on the original setup on Model B, roughly four minutes with the optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol.

Mean of 3 runs, SD whiskers. ≥: mean includes a capped or unfinished run, so the true value is at least this large.

In a recent development, bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Run markers and SD whiskers are approximate reconstructions from the source image; underlying run values and standard deviations were not available.

Mean of 3 runs, SD whiskers. ≥: mean includes a capped or unfinished run, so the true value is at least this large.

Bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Run markers and SD whiskers are approximate reconstructions from the source image; underlying run values and standard deviations were not available.

The investigation also showed how history management affected whether the agent produced an answer at all. Giving GPT‑6.1 Sol more room to retain its browsing history increased the number of runs that produced an answer from three of 18 with the smaller history budget to all 18 with the larger budget, each with the correct answer. For Hidalgo, the business value is giving customers access to faster, more capable models while keeping operating costs sustainable.

Recent findings suggest that asana has released the changes to browser navigation in StackAI and is developing tools to make similar experiments easier to repeat. Over time, the team prepares to incorporate this testing into the platform’s evaluations, so customers and internal teams can compare cost, runtime, and answer quality when configuring their agents.

In a recent development, asana is now using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to test product features before release: Astra navigates the platform, tries different inputs and reports bugs for human QA reviewers. Hidalgo views this as the foundation for a upcoming software development lifecycle, with many cloud agent sessions testing features in parallel.

The complete study is available on the Asana⁠(opens in a new window) and StackAI⁠(opens in a new window) blogs.

Tech Report: Sophos cuts threat investigation time by 96% with OpenAI Daybreak

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (785 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.
  • reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.
  • In a recent development, frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a upcoming window).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.

average response time for cases using AI agents.

reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.

of MDR cases resolved end-to-end by AI.

In a recent development, frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a upcoming window). Advanced models can help defenders find and investigate threats faster. But those capabilities are also spreading to open-weight models, giving attackers new ways to discover vulnerabilities and accelerate exploitation.

Sophos⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) is one of the companies standing in their way, protecting more than 625,000 organisations across sectors and regions. “We see a huge variety of different attacks,” states John Peterson, the manufacturer’s Chief Technology Officer. “We’ve cultivated vast expertise in combating them over four decades in the cybersecurity business.”.

According to recent reports, through OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos is combining OpenAI models with its own threat intelligence, response playbooks and security expertise. The aim isn’t simply to give analysts another tool. It’s to increase the impact of Sophos’s expertise across every customer it protects.

“Sophos brings the domain expertise and the know-how to combat attacks at scale. Programmes like Daybreak, and companies like OpenAI, bring frontier intelligence that allows us to take that domain expertise and scale it to support all of our customers.”.

Recent findings suggest that at the centre of the work is Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-native cyber defense system that includes Sophos Managed Detection and Response (MDR). It brings together sensor data from more than 500 third-party integrations alongside Sophos’s own products. Together, those sensors generate trillions of events every day, which Sophos distills into roughly 1,000 to 2,000 cases for its nine security operations centres to investigate.

It has been revealed that agents built through Daybreak have changed how those cases are handled. An investigation agent gathers the customer context, detections, indicators of compromise (IoCs) and relevant threat intelligence for each case. A planning model then creates a plan–execute–review loop: building an investigation plan, completing the steps and producing a summary with recommended response actions for analysts to review. Other agents can carry out parts of the response.

Before Daybreak, investigating and responding to a case depended primarily on human expertise. Sophos’s existing process averaged around 38 minutes — performance Peterson says was better than 96% of professional security operations centres.

“Now, because of the agents we’ve been able to build through the Daybreak programme, the average response time for cases using those agents has fallen to about 89 seconds. About half of the cases we handle are now being automated by agents we developed using the Daybreak models.”.

Sophos has built customer control into its MDR service through three operating modes:.

Notify: Sophos investigates the case and recommends a response, but the customer acts.

Collaborate: Sophos and the customer work together before action is taken.

Authorise: Sophos can respond directly on the customer’s behalf.

The same boundaries apply whether work is completed by a person or an agent. Sophos uses automation to move quickly and make better use of analysts’ time, but potentially destructive actions still require the right level of human oversight.

“Anything we don’t feel comfortable with an agent handling gets passed off for human judgement,” Peterson confirms.

Reduced the average response time for cases using agents from approximately 38 minutes to 89 seconds.

Enabled Sophos to resolve 52% of MDR cases end-to-end with AI, within boundaries calibrated by Sophos analysts.

Gives customers a faster and more consistent investigation experience.

Helps Sophos scale compute rather than relying on equivalent growth in scarce cybersecurity headcount.

Returns analysts’ attention to the threats, exceptions and decisions where their expertise matters most.

Peterson indicates Sophos will keep expanding what its agents can do. “The response capabilities are going to continue to become more sophisticated, and we’re going to broaden the range of use cases we address with the agents we’ve built.”.

“With programmes like Daybreak, we have an opportunity to stay a step ahead of the attacker community.”.

His advice for other security leaders is simple: “The one thing security leaders should do tomorrow is really come back to focusing on the security fundamentals for their organization,” he says. “That of course includes patching. But patches are only ever going to include vulnerabilities that are known by the vendor.”.

Recent findings suggest that the answer is to maintain “a layered security approach” that includes endpoint protection, multifactor authentication (MFA), network segmentation and strong security operations. “Vulnerabilities are being discovered at an alarming rate and exploited at a scale that we’ve never seen. So I think doing the fundamentals well is more important today than it’s ever been.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT‑6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT‑Image‑2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT‑Live.

Higgsfield AI⁠(opens in a new window) is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea. Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute. Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, users can create videos over 10 minutes long.

Longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work. According to Alex, with models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, it’s now possible for a single creator to execute high-end fashion campaigns from start to finish.

According to recent reports, higgsfield AI’s creative agents take on repetitive production tasks, such as creating multiple variations of a shot. With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling. Alex states that capability helps address one of creative AI’s hardest problems: maintaining consistency across longer videos.

Recent findings suggest that being able to create longer instructional videos also matters to Alex personally. He supports rural schools in Kazakhstan and describes an early effort using GPT‑6 Astra’s visual understanding to identify topics students may be struggling with and create videos tailored to what they need to learn.

For small businesses creating promotional content, having readable text and precise infographics can be just as key as the image itself. GPT‑Image‑2.5 makes that kind of content possible for businesses without large production budgets, Alex says.

“GPT‑Image‑2.5 is state of the art and the first model of its kind that can reliably render the text and infographics on top of the imagery,” he indicates.

In a recent development, higgsfield AI builds its product through close collaboration between around 200 creatives and 100 engineers. Codex gives the creative team “the power of a really strong software engineer,” shares Alex.

Creatives use Codex to turn their ideas into software prototypes. Previously, bringing those prototypes into production required heavy involvement from front-end and back-end engineers. Now, Alex claims GPT‑6 Astra reduces the work needed to bring those ideas into the product.

With less friction between prototyping and production, Alex says Higgsfield AI can develop and ship better products faster.

Industry observers note that next, Higgsfield AI wants creators to be able to describe an idea and see it take shape as they talk. Alex calls that vision “voice to movie,” with AI understanding a creator’s spoken intention and rendering their vision in real time.

It has been revealed that he sees OpenAI’s advances in planning, tool calling, image generation, and voice bringing that experience closer. He describes its voice model as “best in class for voice understanding and just for regular communication.”.

For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.

#30826. The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

📅 14 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (422 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (422 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools.
  • In a recent development, we have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity⁠.
  • This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated owners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT.

In a recent development, we have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity⁠. In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated owners.

Industry observers note that the agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active users of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

But we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

Frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.

The takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies globally⁠(opens in a newly introduced window).

In a recent development, these figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

Analyst-hours per quarter handed back.

Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter.

At Block, the firm behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks.

Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a upcoming teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, indicates. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.”.

Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result.

For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming.

Industry observers note that the team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he states. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path.

Industry observers note that the automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.”.

Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years.

In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy concern on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of concerns. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says.

According to recent reports, another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes.

Sources indicate that finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the glitch lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.”.

While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim states, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.”.

Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises.

Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back.

Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter.

50% boost to triage throughput.

50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations.

It has been revealed that detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly.

As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. That would free security teams to spend less time patching and more time on preventative, strategic work.

“OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by putting these advanced capabilities in everyone’s hands,” he says. “It’s typically only been in very high-profile technology companies and government hands. But everyone, including critical infrastructure, schools, small businesses, can now start utilizing this technology to defend their networks.”.

How Third Moment Research runs 10,000 agents for 36+ hours

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.
  • Recent findings suggest that every manufacturer has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success.
  • The manufacturer is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.

Hours per autonomous research session.

Reduction in backtest time with Codex.

Trillion OpenAI tokens in a single day.

Recent findings suggest that every manufacturer has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success. ⁠(opens in a fresh window)Third Moment Research⁠(opens in a new window) believes the best agents should be really good at that specific work and should improve their capabilities the more they’re used.

The manufacturer is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems. The team uses those scenarios to improve agents, repeating the process as new issues emerge.

Recent findings suggest that codex, GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol support the system’s research and computational work, enabling Third Moment to run 10,000 agents at once on investigations lasting 36-48 hours. The firm also uses Daybreak to test the security of the environments where agents work.

One of Third Moment’s early applications is in the field of quantitative finance given the clear measure of success. This domain provides a concrete setting to study how agents work and where they struggle. The team uses Codex to find and address problems in the research environment.

In one instance, it used Codex with GPT‑5.6, the latest GPT model at the time, to analyze thousands of recorded simulation trajectories (the agents’ actions and the environment’s responses) alongside timestamps and the codebase.

In a recent development, codex uncovered a bottleneck: backtesting a trading strategy across a year of order-level US equity data took several hours. While waiting, agents repeatedly polled for completion, wasting tokens and filling their context with status checks.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling the backtest and analyzing its inputs and usage, Codex identified a caching optimization and a memory-packing technique. It experimented with solutions and deployed the fix to production, reducing the backtest from approximately 3 hours to approximately 3 to 5 minutes. This reduced token use and context pollution, freeing more of the agents’ token budget for further experiments.

It has been revealed that third Moment gives each agent the tools, information, and environment it needs for a specific job. For quantitative research, the team runs the default Codex harness inside a Dockerized environment. Agents receive a terabyte of data, documentation, and a research repository with modules for feature engineering, GPU-supported model training, trading strategies, and simulation.

GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol provide the reasoning, while the Codex harness gives agents tools to act, create prepares, set objectives, spawn subagents, and compact context as work continues.

To address agents that stop before completing a task, Third Moment treats Codex as a subagent within an outer harness powered by GPT‑6 Sol or GPT‑6.1 Sol. The outer harness examines the trajectory when a task is left unfinished and determines whether to retry, terminate the job, or escalate to human review.

Industry observers note that in that research environment, agents work to improve a baseline trading system built by Third Moment’s engineers. They test trading strategies on historical data, assess whether an improvement is meaningful or noise, and use each result to choose the next experiment. According to Adam, their work has improved the baseline trading system.

Industry observers note that before GPT‑5.5, Adam says models could only execute experiments prescribed by a user. With GPT‑5.5 and GPT‑5.6, models working with the Codex harness could use results to design follow-up experiments. Now with GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, agents can investigate root causes through hundreds of experiments running in parallel with subagents.

Sources indicate that that progression has helped agents explore research directions the team hadn’t anticipated. In one session, GPT‑6.1 Sol identified the impact of non-displayed trades on an exchange where those trades accounted for an unexpectedly large share of volume. “This was an unobvious result that our research team did not initially consider,” notes Adam.

In a recent development, third Moment evaluates models across optimization, machine learning systems, and quantitative research. It tests frontier releases at their highest reasoning settings, assessing their ability to navigate repositories, write efficient code, and sustain an investigation. Current testing also includes GPT‑6 Luna.

One benchmark asks agents to reduce a live scoreboard service’s patch latency while preserving its outputs. The team measures speedup by dividing the average runtime of an expert-crafted solution by that of the model’s solution on the same hardware, subject to correctness. GPT‑6 Astra delivered the biggest speedup, according to Adam.

Sources indicate that for targeted work, including checks for specific security weaknesses in the simulation system, the team uses more efficient models like GPT‑5.6 Terra. For deep research, Adam believes stronger reasoning can justify higher cost: “In the space of quantitative finance, the value of finding some interesting signal is extremely high.”.

It has been revealed that with 10,000 agents running autonomously, Third Moment needs a way to test the security of its research environments at scale. The team uses the Daybreak cybersecurity platform to automate that testing before simulations launch.

Industry observers note that the tests check whether an agent could break out of its research environment and access the wider network. “By using Daybreak, we’re able to have agents themselves do penetration testing on the simulation and test the infrastructure and security of it,” claims Adam.

It has been revealed that third Moment’s ambition extends to the specialized work companies do every day. For a retailer, that could mean making better supply chain decisions when inventory is short or a supplier is delayed. For an engineering team, it could mean finding performance bottlenecks in a large codebase. For a document-heavy business, it could mean identifying where commitments in one document don’t match outcomes recorded in another.

Industry observers note that building on the reasoning capabilities of GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Third Moment aims to expand from individual investigations to hundreds of thousands of collaborating subagents. Its roadmap calls for trillions of tokens supporting chains of dozens of dependent experiments, with the goal of using that research to autonomously improve agents as newly introduced challenges arise.

For Adam, this would give people more capacity to shape how agents learn and work: “Humans can be in a much more leveraged position, where they can think about how to do research and optimize the research itself instead of actually doing the research.”.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.

Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.

Sources indicate that reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover new information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, says OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours.

According to recent reports, by reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.”.

Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples.

According to recent reports, stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he claims. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds.

Historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or key threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart indicates. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats.

Faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation.

Sources indicate that comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart says, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.”.

According to recent reports, within SentinelOne, Stewart indicates access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate challenges themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists.

Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security complications as they build.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT‑6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT‑Live‑1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.

According to recent reports, amp⁠(opens in a latest window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages.

Recent findings suggest that amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its customers, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.”.

It has been revealed that as builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp people consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of.

To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn indicates it gives Amp owners access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task.

“Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he states. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to plan, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship.

Amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn indicates. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for new consumers and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels.

For that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards.

In a recent development, quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the intends for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he says.

Amp recently announced Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem.

It has been revealed that with Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, customers can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run.

In a recent development, amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn says the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result.

For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn claims.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.

For lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities. The firm’s Agreement Analyzer brings those inputs into a single review workflow, producing analysis and proposed changes that lawyers can inspect and refine.

According to recent reports, though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage. “Now, we’re seeing many more opportunities for use in challenging legal tasks such as deep analysis of complex agreements,” he says.

Agreement Analyzer helps lawyers compare corresponding provisions across precedents and track how those provisions interact.

It has been revealed that sullivan & Cromwell partner John Savva developed Agreement Analyzer as a single-user proof of concept built with Codex. He then collaborated with OpenAI on improving the quality of outputs, enhancing efficiency through parallel processing and transforming the application into a tool that could be used by multiple lawyers at the same time.

Agreement Analyzer integrates Sullivan & Cromwell’s workflows, curated firm precedents, negotiating playbooks and ChatGPT Enterprise. After inputting a draft agreement into the tool, a lawyer can add their own selected precedents and a playbook with firm and client positions, as well as information on market practice. The tool performs multiple review cycles from different perspectives, synthesizes the outputs, helps identify potential issues and returns a memorandum and proposed tracked changes for a lawyer to review, adapt or reject.

Savva emphasizes that what makes an AI tool’s output trustworthy is full transparency. “If an AI tool makes a claim about market practice, you need to be able to see the source of that information,” he indicates.

Savva describes an application in which agents develop conclusions and other agents challenge them in an adversarial process. In a potential use case, specialized agents review the agreement in parallel for such things as market deviations and risk allocation, interactions between clauses, and ambiguities that could impact litigation. The results distinguish findings supported after challenge by other agents, dismissed findings, and unverified issues retained with qualifications. Lawyers can inspect the issues, their supporting explanations, and the relevant precedents, then decide which findings warrant changes in the final markup.

Sources indicate that sullivan & Cromwell is continuing to explore tools shaped around specific legal tasks. For Savva, stronger analytical capabilities create an opportunity to support more of the research and writing process.

Savva points to advances in reasoning capabilities with GPT‑6 Astra: “Astra’s really moved things forward in terms of the quality of the reasoning that’s available, and that has been the bottleneck in the past,” he indicates.

Teaching students to think and learn through questions

📅 15 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (410 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that on Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn.
  • Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.
  • It has been revealed that today, we are launching the AI for Educators⁠(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that on Teachers’ Day, we celebrate those who help us learn. A good question can change the course of a lesson. It can bring an unspoken question to light, open up another way to solve a problem, or help someone recognize what they already know. Teachers do this work every day: they know their students, choose how to introduce an idea, and guide them from their first attempt to understanding.

Set in a university classroom, the campaign takes a humorous look at the changing relationship between teachers and students and celebrates the role of educators in a world with AI.

It has been revealed that today, we are launching the AI for Educators⁠(opens in a new window) course in Brazilian Portuguese on OpenAI Academy, OpenAI’s free learning platform. Designed for educators in primary, secondary, and higher education, the course highlights how to use AI to proposal lessons, create activities and assessments, and prepare communications while preserving educators’ pedagogical judgment.

Study Mode helps you explore a subject⁠(opens in a new window) step by step, with questions, hints, explanations, and checks for understanding. Developed in collaboration with teachers, scientists, and experts in pedagogy, the feature aims to encourage active participation and reflection on one’s own reasoning.

To turn on Study Mode, select Study from the tools menu in ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that A student reviewing biology, for example, might ask: “I’m studying enzymes. Ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and help me identify what I need to review.”.

Teachers can also try Study Mode with subjects they know well, looking at whether the questions encourage reasoning and whether the explanations are appropriate for their class.

In a science lesson on evaporation, for example, a teacher might ask students to investigate why clothes dry on a clothesline. After exploring the topic with Study Mode, each student writes their own explanation and a question to discuss in class, without referring back to the conversation. The teacher can use these responses to identify what needs to be revisited with the class.

In a recent development, this Teachers’ Day, we invite you to experiment: explore the AI for Educators course, try Study Mode, and discover how these tools can be useful in different teaching contexts. Technology can open up newly introduced ways to learn, but it is teachers who know their students, ask the most important questions, and help turn curiosity into knowledge.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing the Rosalind Academic Strategy, offering eligible labs sponsored access to GPT‑Rosalind and tools for life sciences discovery.

According to recent reports, we’re introducing the Rosalind Academic Plan to help more academic scientists access GPT‑Rosalind⁠, our dedicated life sciences model, which combines frontier reasoning with Rosalind workbench⁠(opens in a new window) that enables specialized tool orchestration across medicinal chemistry, genomics, wet-lab assistance, and other scientific applications. Eligible labs can receive up to 30 Business Standard seats at no cost for up to 12 months, with access to GPT‑Rosalind subject to trusted-access approval.

In a recent development, academic research creates knowledge that entire fields build on. Work that begins with a fundamental question about biology can eventually change how we diagnose disease, develop medicines, or grow food. But those advances depend on scientists having the resources to explore ideas, test them, and share what they learn.

Industry observers note that accelerating scientific discovery is central to OpenAI’s mission of ensuring that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. With this blueprint, we’re investing in the scientists doing that foundational work—helping more labs combine their expertise and judgment with AI tools built for life sciences research.

Many of the advances we rely on today grew out of years of basic research.

The Human Genome Project helped launch modern genomics, transforming medicine, diagnostics, and biotechnology.

Curiosity-driven work on bacterial immune systems led to CRISPR-Cas9, which revolutionized genome editing and is now advancing research in cancer, inherited disease, agriculture, and biotechnology. Decades of university research on mRNA also laid the groundwork for COVID-19 vaccines and a upcoming generation of vaccines and therapies.

Industry observers note that academic research has always laid the groundwork for advances in medicine and biotechnology. By helping more scientists combine their scientific expertise and judgment with the advanced specialized reasoning of GPT‑Rosalind, we hope to support discoveries whose benefits reach far beyond the lab.

OpenAI is committed to enabling academic researchers to pursue their scientific ambitions. Distinguished academic labs are already exploring how GPT‑Rosalind can support work ranging from protein design to understanding neurodegeneration. These examples show where researchers are applying the model within their scientific workflows.

With the newly introduced Rosalind Academic Strategy, academic researchers can bring GPT‑Rosalind and Rosalind Workbench to their lab with greater flexibility and harness frontier model intelligence for scientific research.

Access to all commercially available frontier OpenAI models, subject to plan usage limits.

Research data shared through the Rosalind Academic Plan is not used to train our models by default.

GPT‑Rosalind is a specialized life sciences model designed to support deeper reasoning on complex biological questions. Through trusted access, approved researchers can use it to investigate sensitive scientific questions within safeguards designed for legitimate research.

Designing candidate drugs, therapeutic proteins, peptides, and enzymes, and optimizing their molecular interactions, selectivity, stability, and suitability for development.

Identifying molecular signatures of disease and developing liquid biopsies and other minimally invasive diagnostics to detect disease earlier, monitor progression, and assess treatment response.

Designing and evaluating antibodies and vaccines against emerging viral variants, investigating host–pathogen interactions, and studying the strength and durability of protective immune responses.

Developing approaches to correcting genetic defects and modulating gene expression, designing RNA therapeutics, and investigating how to deliver treatments safely and effectively to intended tissues.

Investigating crop resilience, plant disease, and animal health, and applying genetic, nutritional, and biological insights to improve food production and veterinary care.

Studying biodiversity, adaptation, species interactions, and environmental exposures to understand ecosystem change and inform conservation, bioremediation, and responses to climate change.

Studying how microorganisms resist antibiotics, antivirals, and antifungals, and developing new treatments for resistant infections, biofilms, and persistent disease.

Card 1 of 7: Drug and protein design.

According to recent reports, the Rosalind Academic Plan is currently available to academic labs at U.S. universities. PIs and lab leads at universities without an OpenAI Enterprise agreement can apply on behalf of their labs through our trusted access process. Labs at universities with an existing agreement must apply through their university’s Enterprise access process.

Once approved, PIs and lab leads can activate free access to GPT‑Rosalind for up to 30 named members, alongside the other OpenAI frontier models included in the initiative. API access is not included at this time. Verified PIs and lab leads manage member permissions and are responsible for their lab’s approved use.

Assess the lab’s institutional affiliation, research activities, and intended use.

Establish clear responsibilities for the lab lead and a designated institutional safety contact.

Safeguards continue after activation through monitoring and enforcement. For registered high-sensitivity use cases, our safety checks account for the approved research context. When questions arise, we may follow up with researchers to clarify the work and confirm authorization. This approach is designed to detect potential misuse while accounting for legitimate research context and reducing unnecessary interruptions to authorized work.

We’re starting with academic labs as part of a broader effort to put useful AI tools in the hands of more scientists. By lowering the cost of access, we hope to give more researchers room to pursue ideas whose benefits could reach far beyond their own labs—from a clearer understanding of disease to better treatments and more resilient food systems.

Those advances will come from scientists asking crucial questions and doing the work to answer them. We want to help more of them do that work.

If you’re affiliated with an academic lab, learn more about the Rosalind Academic Plan and check whether you’re eligible⁠(opens in a new window).

  • More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.
  • Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.

More agents created with the ChatGPT plugin.

More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin.

Maximum reduction in time to build one connector, from 3–6 weeks to 4 days.

Industry observers note that people and AI agents need context to get work done, but it’s usually scattered across systems, from Slack to Google Docs. Finding it and understanding how it all fits together can be a challenge.

That’s why Stack Overflow⁠(opens in a latest window) is building a knowledge intelligence platform that unifies those sources and turns raw context into verified knowledge available wherever people and agents work.

Industry observers note that openAI models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol power the platform’s AI, with tasks routing to different models based on the reasoning required and cost. Codex helps the manufacturer’s engineers build the products, while a ChatGPT plugin makes their newer agentic product, Stack Overflow for Agents, easier to discover and use.

Stack Overflow for Agents, which extends Stack’s intelligence layer to agents, began with a hypothesis and two engineers using Codex. The engineers gave Codex a development environment and a plan, and then worked with it to build the product. Within a few weeks, Alex notes, they had a full-fledged product.

In a recent development, “So it really made their team feel bigger,” Alex claims. “They were able to throw a container at it and say, ‘This is our blueprint, help us build it.’”.

In a recent development, stack Internal, Stack Overflow’s enterprise product, needs to connect to all the systems where organizations keep their knowledge. Building this capability requires more human involvement than the two-engineer effort behind Stack Overflow for Agents, but Codex is accelerating this work, too.

Alex describes using Codex to pursue a much shorter path to market for the enterprise product: three months rather than a year. Building connectors is one concrete example.

Industry observers note that more recently, the team built a connector in a single day. By accelerating connectors, Codex helps Stack Overflow bring enterprise products to market faster.

In a recent development, once Stack Overflow for Agents was ready for distribution, the team needed a way to get it into people’s workflows. It built a ChatGPT plugin so users could discover and set up the product in ChatGPT, with fewer steps than a traditional Model Context Protocol (MCP) setup.

Alex notes the plugin tripled registrations and accelerated agent creation: “I think we were up to 10X last time I checked.”.

Stack Overflow manages its own model routing and configuration, but Alex hopes to explore using the Decisions API to reduce some of that work and put more engineering capacity into the product.

“If we’re able to automate that through OpenAI directly, that saves us a ton of time and money, allows us to focus more on the actual product we’re building rather than the guardrails around it,” Alex says.

Stack Overflow is also working on expanding its knowledge product to enable sharing of what people learn. To date, its focus has been pulling information in. Now, Alex is closing the loop so knowledge gained in a one-to-one session with a developer or someone outside engineering can help others, too.

Recent findings suggest that “As I’m learning, how do I make sure that the rest of my organization is learning with me?”, said Alex. “I’m really looking forward to building a product that allows for that full knowledge life cycle.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.

First BDC mark tracker version; ~10–12 total development hours, including refinements.

First-pass credit agreement analysis, followed by 1+ hour of human review.

At Benefit Street Partners, a credit-focused investment manager, answering an investment committee’s follow-up questions used to take days or weeks. Portfolio manager Anant Kumar says analysts can now turn a round of comments in a day with Codex, and often answer questions during the meeting itself. BSP is using these tools to add more review capacity and rigor to underwriting within the same timeframe, rather than to do more deals.

To create a dashboard he could share with colleagues, Kumar used to need someone with software expertise to build a website and pull in the data. Now he builds his own tools, using AI to draft code and review it for errors.

In a recent development, his tracker uses public SEC filings from business development companies (BDCs) to compare how firms value the same loan. The team can see how its marks compare with other holders’ valuations.

It has been revealed that kumar built the tracker and used Codex for code review. The first version took a day. After adding features and refining the interface over subsequent weeks, he estimates total development time at 10–12 hours total.

Industry observers note that kumar’s other tool analyzes credit agreements, which are often 300 pages or longer. Investors need to find clauses that could shift value away from lenders, a task that previously meant asking outside counsel to work through the agreement page by page. Kumar brought together memos from leading law firms on clauses and risks to watch for. He describes the analyzer as a “second brain within our organization.”.

An uploaded credit agreement takes about 20 minutes to process into a first-pass analysis, followed by an hour or more of human review. BSP has refactored the tool with GPT‑6 Astra, and it is now live in the company-hosted portal.

“The AI is very helpful in collating data, ingesting it, synthesizing analysis, but the ultimate investment decision needs to be made by a human,” he indicates.

Underwriting is typically a multi-round process. A round consists of further diligence and a revised memo responding to the investment committee’s questions. Deal timelines range from a few days to a few weeks, so the number of rounds varies. Kumar claims, “We feel more confident in our decision making because we have more information at our disposal.”.

Built the first BDC tracker in a day, using Codex for code review; about 10–12 hours total including later additions.

Produces a first-pass analysis of a credit agreement in about 20 minutes, followed by an hour or more of human review.

Answers committee follow-up questions faster with Codex, often during the meeting, according to Kumar.

Sources indicate that BSP is working to connect information across deals. Continuous underwriting is a longer-term aspiration: the team could monitor loans as news happens and examine the effects across its portfolio, rather than re-underwriting only after an event.

“Codex has unlocked my day, because I have many more hours in the day to do more high-level work and less routine work,” notes Kumar.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Almost 50 years after starting in a compounding pharmacy in Paraná, the group operates a proprietary agent platform that autonomously resolves up to 80% of resellers’ operational requests—enabling the sales force to take on an advisory role.

autonomous resolution of operational requests.

of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise covered since November 2025.
